newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest crops probably survived frost.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest crops probably survived frost.

text.p: U.S. Midwest crops probably were not damaged by scattered frost late Wednesday and early Thursday from Indiana to Ohio, meteorologists said.
"The crop itself will generate enough warmth to prevent harm," said Joel Burgio, Weather Services Corp meteorologist.
Burgio said lows mostly ranged from 35 to 37 degrees Fahrenheit from Illinois to Ohio, with isolated cases of 31 to 32 degrees in northern Indiana and Michigan.
"It was a little cooler than I expected. These temperatures were capable of generating frost," he said.

The coldest weather stretched from east central and northeast Illinois through northwest Indiana and into southern Michigan and northwest Ohio. Lows in the low 30s could recur Thursday night and early Friday in Michigan and Ohio, but after that, the Midwest will warm up with highs Friday in the 70s, meteorologists said.

"They may have had a little bit of frost...but I don't think it was there long enough (to hurt crops)," said Fred Gesser, Weather Express Inc meteorologist. "Plants can maintain two to three degrees of their own heat."

The Midwest warms up Friday with highs in the 70s in western Midwest and again in the eastern areas Saturday. Normal to below normal temperatures return Sunday and should remain through much of next week with highs ranging from the upper 60s to low 70s, meteorologists said.
Daily rain amounts of 0.5 to 2.5 inches were forecast from southern Minnesota to eastern Missouri throughout Illinois Saturday to Monday, said Gesser.
"I think, potentially, it's going to be a wet three to five days," Gesser said.
WSC's Burgio also forecast rain for that area, but said amounts may range from 0.25 to 1.0 inch Friday through Sunday.
More showers and cool weather were likely early next week, but by midweek it should turn dry with temperatures rising to normal levels, he said.
